extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners and litigators (IPR counsel), patent examiners, and parties participating in PTAB IPR proceedings
extracted.subtask_short: IPR written description and obviousness analysis
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and evidentiary criteria used in PTAB IPR decisions to evaluate written description/priority entitlement, anticipation, obviousness, and objective indicia (nexus, coextensiveness, commensurateness) for gene-therapy-related patent claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description requirement (§112(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: To be entitled to the filing date of an earlier provisional application, the earlier application must disclose the claimed invention “in the manner provided by § 112(a) (other than the requirement to disclose the best mode).” Section 112(a) requires that the specification contain a written description of the claimed invention. “[T]he hallmark of written description is disclosure.” (Ariad).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The specification must contain a written description of the claimed invention; courts look to whether the earlier application discloses the claimed invention under §112(a). See Ariad Pharm., Inc. v. Eli Lilly & Co., 598 F.3d 1336, 1351 (Fed. Cir. 2010) (en banc).

rubrics_metrics.name: Possession standard for written description
rubrics_metrics.description: The written description requirement is met when the specification “conveys to those skilled in the art that the inventor had possession of” and “actually invented” the claimed subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask whether the disclosure would allow a person of ordinary skill to clearly conclude that the inventor invented the claimed invention as of the asserted priority date (Lockwood: must describe an invention in sufficient detail). The focus is on what the spec reasonably conveys to the artisan, not later inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description cannot be established by obviousness or speculation
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not sufficient for the written description requirement that the disclosure, when combined with the knowledge in the art, would lead one to speculate as to modifications that the inventor might have envisioned but failed to disclose. “Obviousness simply is not enough; the subject matter must be disclosed to establish possession.” (PowerOasis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conflate obviousness and written description: evidence that the claimed subject matter would have been obvious does not establish that the earlier spec showed possession. Avoid relying on inferences from knowledge in the art to supply missing disclosure for possession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description of specific quantitative limitations (e.g., expression levels)
rubrics_metrics.description: For limitations reciting particular expression levels or numeric ranges, the earlier application must disclose those levels or otherwise convey possession of those specific quantitative limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General statements about low or higher activity are insufficient if no numerical levels or enabling examples are provided. The absence of gene therapy examples or numerical expression data in the earlier application supports a finding of inadequate written description for claimed expression-level limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description must support specific vector/type limitations (e.g., AAV vs adenovirus)
rubrics_metrics.description: A disclosure of dosing or particles/kg for one viral family (e.g., adenovirus) does not necessarily provide written description support for claims directed to a different viral family (e.g., adeno-associated virus, AAV).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Units or particles/kg alone do not bridge different vector families. The specification must convey that the inventor possessed administering the particular vector type claimed; expert testimony that dosing for one vector ‘does not inform’ dosing for another supports non-support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure modality must match claim modality (protein replacement vs gene therapy)
rubrics_metrics.description: A disclosure of dosages or regimens for protein replacement therapy does not necessarily describe the claimed invention of gene therapy (i.e., expressed polypeptide levels resulting from in vivo expression after vector administration).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the earlier spec relates to administered protein amounts or to in vivo expression levels from gene therapy; sharing a common therapeutic goal is not sufficient to establish written description for a different modality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority entitlement depends on adequate written description
rubrics_metrics.description: If the earlier application does not provide adequate written description support for the claimed limitations, the claims are not entitled to the earlier filing date and instead take the later patent's filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal consequence: lacking written description, earlier provisional cannot be relied upon for priority; this can render intervening references prior art under §102(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective indicia of nonobviousness (secondary considerations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Objective evidence of non-obviousness may include long-felt need and failure of others, industry praise and copying, and unexpected results; such evidence “may often be the most probative and cogent evidence in the record.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider these factors, but they do not automatically control the obviousness analysis; strong prima facie obviousness can outweigh secondary considerations (e.g., Pfizer v. Apotex). List of typical categories: long-felt need/failure, praise/copying, unexpected results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nexus requirement for objective indicia
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee must establish a nexus between the objective evidence and the merits of the claimed invention; the patentee bears the burden of establishing that nexus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nexus means a legally and factually sufficient connection such that the objective evidence should be considered in determining non-obviousness. If the evidence is directed to something other than what is both claimed and novel, nexus is lacking (ClassCo; Merck & Cie).

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of nexus and coextensiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee is entitled to a presumption of nexus when the patentee shows the asserted objective evidence is tied to a specific product and that product ‘embodies the claimed features, and is coextensive with them.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the marketed product embodies the claimed features and is coextensive (i.e., product is the invention disclosed and claimed), nexus is presumed and the burden shifts to the party asserting obviousness to rebut. Coextensive means the product is essentially the claimed invention and unclaimed features are insignificant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commensurate-in-scope requirement for nexus
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no nexus unless the evidence presented is ‘reasonably commensurate with the scope of the claims.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence directed to a narrow aspect (e.g., a single mutation) may fail to be commensurate with broad claims that cover many variants, capsids, promoters, or sequences. Courts equate coextensiveness with commensurate-in-scope in evaluating presumptions of nexus (Fox Factory, Zaxcom).

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative route to prove nexus without presumption
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when a presumption of nexus is inappropriate, a patent owner may still prove nexus by showing the secondary-considerations evidence is the direct result of the unique characteristics of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent owner must identify the unique characteristics and provide evidence linking the objective indicia directly to those characteristics (Fox Factory quoting In re Huang). Mere industry praise directed to an element already in the prior art will not suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation and weight of objective indicia in context
rubrics_metrics.description: Objective indicia must be weighed in the context of whether the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious to a skilled artisan; they may be the most probative evidence yet can be insufficient if the prima facie case of obviousness is strong.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider objective indicia alongside the Graham factors and the totality of the evidence; lack of nexus or commensurateness diminishes their weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivation to combine and reasonable expectation of success
rubrics_metrics.description: For an obviousness conclusion based on combining references, a person of ordinary skill in the art must have been motivated to combine the references and have a reasonable expectation of success in doing so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show why a skilled artisan would select and combine particular teachings (e.g., a preferred variant with a commonly used vector) and whether prior art or common practice would make success reasonably expected. Evidence that a particular approach (e.g., AAV vectors for hemophilia B) was common supports motivation and expectation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden and standard of proof in IPR proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Petitioner must prove invalidity grounds (anticipation, obviousness) by a preponderance of the evidence in an IPR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PTAB decisions will state when a petitioner 'has proven by a preponderance of the evidence' that claims are anticipated or obvious. Use record citations and witness testimony to meet this burden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction influences validity analysis (e.g., definition of 'treating')
rubrics_metrics.description: How claim terms are construed (for example, ‘treating’ construed to include partial alleviation of symptoms) materially affects anticipation/obviousness analyses and whether prior art discloses or renders the claim obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit claim constructions adopted in the proceeding should be applied consistently when assessing prior art teachings and whether those teachings satisfy claim limitations.
